arXiv:2606.01643v2 [cs.CV] 03 Nov 2026

Conditional Collapse in Sign Language Production:
A Diagnostic and a Coverage Argument

Rui Hong Affiliation: George Mason University    Jana Košecká Affiliation: {rhong5, kosecka}@gmu.edu
Abstract

The goal of Sign Language Production (SLP) is to translate natural language text into corresponding sign language movements performed by a virtual avatar. The quality of the generated motion is typically evaluated by a motion-space Fréchet distance (FID) and back-translation BLEU score on benchmarks such as How2Sign [5]. The existing approaches can improve both metrics substantially while the underlying generator fails to represent the input sentence — a failure we call conditional collapse. In this work we propose to evaluate the generated motion at three independent levels: (τ1\tau_{1}) initial-pose conditioning, (τ2\tau_{2}) output diversity, and (τ3\tau_{3}) target faithfulness. We compute these as pairwise-distance ratios using latent representations of a frozen motion autoencoder (MoAE), judged against each dataset’s own GT-vs-GT reference. We evaluate diffusion and regression SLP models on How2Sign, including a re-implemented Neural Sign Actors, and show that τ3\tau_{3} faithfulness is never attained, while FID varies by nearly two orders of magnitude and is uncorrelated with faithfulness. We then apply the same models and diagnostic to Phoenix-2014T, CSL-Daily, and gloss-level ASL3DWord and show that faithfulness varies proportionally to how densely the training sentences cover the test conditions (conditioning coverage) and not corpus size. The smaller but densely covered Phoenix-2014T and ASL3DWord datasets generate faithful sign motion, while CSL-Daily follows the input text yet falls short of sign language faithfulness. Using the largest, open-domain How2Sign dataset, the models collapse at every scale. We introduce two measurements of the text data that rank the corpora in the order of how densely the training sentences fill the embedding space, and how close each test sentence lies to its nearest training sentence.

1 Introduction

Sign Language Production (SLP) systems generate avatar sign language motion from text [19, 1, 24, 26, 29] and report steady benchmark gains. Reliable evaluation requires metrics that respond to whether each output is faithful to its specific input, not merely plausible under the training distribution. We study this requirement in sentence-level SLP, where systems on How2Sign [5] report improving Fréchet distance (FID) over motion features and back-translation (BT) BLEU. We argue that both headline metrics can rise while the generator remains essentially text-independent. FID rewards an anatomically valid mean motion that ignores the input over a model that follows the input but produces slightly noisier motion; it can thus prefer a collapsed generator over a faithful one, as we observe on How2Sign (Sec. 5.2). On How2Sign, BT-BLEU is bounded by the BT model. Without pretraining, How2Sign alone does not train a usable translator, and the BT model collapses to high-frequency boilerplate, reflecting token-frequency overlap rather than motion–text correspondence.

Beyond detecting this failure, we ask what drives it. Our answer is a coverage argument: whether a generator learns to condition on text is governed by conditioning coverage — whether semantically close training sentences recur often enough in the conditioning space for the text-to-motion correspondence to be learnable. We show a corpus with 3131K paired sentences collapsing while a 77K-sentence corpus with denser coverage does not.

Contributions. (i) Given any text-to-motion model and a held-out test set, we encode both ground-truth motions and model generations through a frozen motion autoencoder MoAE (a small transformer) trained once on the target dataset’s ground-truth motions, compressing each motion into a compact latent vector and reconstructing it. We then compute three pairwise-distance ratios in that space, varying the sentence conditioning and comparing the generated and ground-truth motions; faithfulness is judged against the dataset’s own measured GT-vs-GT reference rather than a fixed threshold (Sec. 3.1), and a frame-level DTW check against a human–human alignability baseline sharpens the verdict (Sec. 6.2). (ii) We identify three indicators of conditional collapse at different levels: an initial-pose level (τ1\tau_{1}), an output diversity level (τ2\tau_{2}), and a faithfulness level (τ3\tau_{3}) that can be attained independently, with visual and quantitative evidence (Sec. 4). (iii) We run the same architectures, recipe, and diagnostic across four datasets spanning a coverage spectrum: open-domain How2Sign, weather-domain Phoenix-2014T [6], daily-domain CSL-Daily [27], and isolated-gloss ASL3DWord [4], supported by measurements of the text data alone (Sec. 6). Controls (text shuffling, frozen-encoder swaps) rule out the text encoder; a retrained Progressive Transformers [19] collapsing on densely-covered Phoenix shows coverage is necessary but not sufficient.

The failures we document are diagnosable: report the diagnostic ratios alongside FID and BT-BLEU, judge them against per-dataset GT-vs-GT references, and be transparent about the coverage properties of the training corpus.

2 Related Work

Sign Language Production. Existing sentence-level SLP approaches fall into two families. Regression based models, such as Progressive Transformers (PT) [19] decode poses autoregressively with a learned step counter; Huang et al. [10] decode non-autoregressively with a graph-convolutional pose generator; T2S-GPT [26] generates dynamic-length VQ pose codes autoregressively. A representative Diffusion-based model, MDM [21], is a transformer denoiser on frozen CLIP conditioning; G2P-DDM [24] runs discrete diffusion in a VQ latent; Neural Sign Actors (NSA) [1] is a GNN++LSTM denoiser on SMPL-X parameters. Hong and Kosecka [9] report usable MDM-style generation at the gloss level on ASL3DWord [4] (a WLASL [13] subset); Signs as Tokens (SOKE) [29] generates part-wise discrete sign tokens with a pretrained language model across How2Sign, Phoenix-2014T, and CSL-Daily, augmented by retrieving word-level signs from external dictionaries — which we read as independent evidence for the coverage account of Sec. 6: word-level signs are injected because sentence-level pairs alone do not cover the conditions. We use SOKE’s released SMPL-X fittings as paired data (its generator weights are unreleased).

Sign Language Translation and BT evaluation. SLP approaches are commonly scored by back-translating generated motion and reporting BLEU translation score. On How2Sign, no-pretraining translators plateau near BLEU-4 1.21.2 [22], reaching 8.038.03 with I3D features [20] and ∼\sim1212 only after 1111K-hour pretraining [22]; our own BT model plateaus at ≈2.5\approx 2.5 even on GT motion. PT [19] and NSA [1] report scores of 10.5110.51 and 13.1213.12 without pretraining, while independent retrainings place PT at 1.61.6–4.44.4 [10, 24, 26] and note its dependence on GT timing.

Evaluation critiques. FID’s limitations for conditional generation are known in text-to-image [12] and text-to-motion [7] domains, motivating paired R-precision and multimodality metrics. Our diagnostic targets the conditional-mean collapse blindness dominant in SLP and calibrates its verdicts against per-dataset GT-vs-GT references. Pose-space DTW distances (DTW-MJE) are standard on Phoenix-2014T [19, 10, 26] but are reported without a human–human baseline, which Sec. 6.2 supplies. Jiang et al. [11] meta-evaluate pose-based sign language metrics by correlation with human judgment; we instead diagnose why generators fail.

3 Diagnostic Approach

Let fθf_{\theta} be any Sign Language Production (SLP) model, regression or diffusion-based, that takes a sentence in natural language and generates a sequence of human poses. Consider {(ti,mi)}i=1N\{(t_{i},m_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} the full test set, where tit_{i} is the ii-th text input and mi∈ℝT×Dm_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D} its ground-truth motion clip. Let ϕ:ℝT×D→ℝd\phi:\mathbb{R}^{T\times D}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a frozen motion autoencoder MoAE, with latent dimension d=256d=256. We use T=100T=100 frames, per-frame D=44​ upper-body joints×3=132D=44\text{ upper-body joints}\times 3=132 pelvis-relative 33D coordinates, and train one MoAE per dataset on its train motions only (see architecture in Appendix D). Define zi:=ϕ⁡(fθ​(ti,s1))z_{i}:=\phi(f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{1})) as the latent representation of SLP model output, and zi∗:=ϕ⁡(mi)z_{i}^{*}:=\phi(m_{i}), the MoAE encoded GT motion for the associated text sentence. We compute the following pairwise statistics:

dinter\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{inter}} =𝔼i≠j​‖zi−zj‖2,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i\neq j}\,\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|_{2}, (1)
dintra\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{intra}} =𝔼i​‖ϕ⁡(fθ​(ti,s1))−ϕ⁡(fθ​(ti,s2))‖2.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\,\big\|\phi(f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{1}))-\phi(f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{2}))\big\|_{2}. (2)

Here s1≠s2s_{1}\neq s_{2} are two independent sampling seeds of a stochastic (diffusion) generator; a deterministic (regression) model takes no seed, so fθ​(ti,s1)=fθ​(ti,s2)f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{1})=f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{2}).

dinter​-​GT\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{inter\text{-}GT}} =𝔼i≠j​‖zi∗−zj∗‖2,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i\neq j}\,\|z_{i}^{*}-z_{j}^{*}\|_{2}, (3)
dpair\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{pair}} =𝔼i​‖zi−zi∗‖2,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\,\|z_{i}-z_{i}^{*}\|_{2}, (4)
dpair​-​rand\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{pair\text{-}rand}} =𝔼i​‖zi−zπ⁡(i)∗‖2.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\,\|z_{i}-z_{\pi(i)}^{*}\|_{2}. (5)

Here π\pi randomly shuffles {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\}, leaving no index in place, so zπ⁡(i)∗z_{\pi(i)}^{*} is the GT motion of a different test sample.

Only dinterd_{\mathrm{inter}} and dpaird_{\mathrm{pair}} capture how the output pose is affected by the input sentence and whether it lands on the correct target; dintrad_{\mathrm{intra}} isolates pure sampling noise, so input-driven variation can be told apart from it; dinter​-​GTd_{\mathrm{inter\text{-}GT}} measures how much the GT motions of different sentences naturally differ, so a small dinterd_{\mathrm{inter}} signals collapse only when it is small compared to this natural spread; and dpair​-​randd_{\mathrm{pair\text{-}rand}} measures whether the generated SLP output is closer to another example other than its own GT.

Three diagnostic ratios. From these statistics we form three unitless quantities: a condition ratio (input-driven variance vs. sampling noise), a diversity ratio (output variance vs. GT cross-sentence variance), and a faithfulness ratio (target alignment vs. a random-GT baseline):

ρcond\displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{cond}} =dinter/dintra,\displaystyle=d_{\mathrm{inter}}/d_{\mathrm{intra}}, (6)
ρdiv\displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{div}} =dinter/dinter​-​GT,\displaystyle=d_{\mathrm{inter}}/d_{\mathrm{inter\text{-}GT}}, (7)
ρfaith\displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} =dpair/dpair​-​rand.\displaystyle=d_{\mathrm{pair}}/d_{\mathrm{pair\text{-}rand}}. (8)

Since ρcond\rho_{\mathrm{cond}} requires a stochastic sampling, a deterministic model has dintra=0d_{\mathrm{intra}}=0 (no seed dependence), making ρcond\rho_{\mathrm{cond}} undefined. The other two ratios only need a single generation per sentence, so they still apply; for deterministic models we report ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}} and ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} only.

FID measures a Fréchet distance between two unconditional Gaussians fit to feature distributions: a model whose outputs cluster around the GT marginal mean attains small FID even when individual outputs fθ​(ti)f_{\theta}(t_{i}) are not faithful motion representing their input tit_{i}. The guideline of ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} approaching 1.01.0 captures this failure mode directly. The diagnostic requires no new training (it reuses one frozen MoAE and O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) pairwise distances on the full test split) and costs at most one extra forward pass per sentence (the second seed for dintrad_{\mathrm{intra}}; none for deterministic models).

3.1 Per-dataset GT-vs-GT reference

To interpret ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} we need a reference value. It is not zero. Two genuine human renditions of the same sentence differ in signer, speed, and style. For sentences that are signed by at least two signers, we can measure

ρfaith,ref=𝔼g,k≠k′​‖zgk∗−zgk′∗‖𝔼g≠g′,k,k′​‖zgk∗−zgk′′∗‖,\rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{g,\,k\neq k^{\prime}}\|z^{*}_{g_{k}}-z^{*}_{g_{k^{\prime}}}\|}{\mathbb{E}_{g\neq g^{\prime},\,k,k^{\prime}}\|z^{*}_{g_{k}}-z^{*}_{g^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}}\|}, (9)

where gg indexes same-text groups and kk renditions within a group: the numerator is the distance between two renditions of the same sentence, the denominator the distance across different sentences. It shows how close a second human rendition comes to the target, measured from each dataset’s own ground truth. It is an empirical reference, not a lower bound. A generator that outputs the average of the valid renditions can fall below it without modeling how signing varies.

Because ρfaith,ref\rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} differs across datasets, we propose no absolute threshold for ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}. A model far above its dataset’s ρfaith,ref\rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} has collapsed. Reaching the reference is consistent with faithful generation but does not prove it. Table 1 lists the measured references and the pairs behind them; CSL-Daily, built from scripted cross-signer re-performances, is the strictest. How2Sign’s remaining exact repeats are short greetings/fillers (“Hi!”, “Okay?”) whose clips carry no sentence-specific motion and would push the reference to ≈1.0\approx 1.0, so we restrict to ≥5\geq 5-word cross-video repeats.

3.2 Stability of the diagnostic

The numbers in Tab. 3 use the full test split of each dataset, so the reported values do not depend on which subsample of test sentences is drawn. Even on the full test split, almost every sentence-level model evaluated on How2Sign attains ρfaith≈1\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1. A fair concern is that this value reflects a problem with the metric itself, not with the models: either (i) the MoAE cannot tell motions apart in its latent space, or (ii) ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} always returns ≈1\approx 1 regardless of input. We rule both out with two checks, and add a third on what the MoAE resolves.

(1) MoAE initialization. Re-training the MoAE from a different random initialization (same architecture and data) and re-running the diagnostic preserves the relative ordering of all measured checkpoints; the diagnostic is robust to MoAE training noise and not an artefact of one particular MoAE fit.

(2) GT-vs-GT check: can ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} ever move? To rule out (ii), we feed the diagnostic the strongest possible “alignment” case: a second GT rendition of the same sentence in place of the model output. This yields the references of Sec. 3.1 (0.670.67–0.870.87), far below 11, and the healthy models of Sec. 6 reach them: the metric can move; the collapsed models do not move it.

(3) MoAE resolution on hands. Per-joint-group reconstruction error (normalized RMSE, the fraction of motion not captured) on full test splits: body/arms 0.170.17–0.200.20, hands 0.300.30–0.370.37 — hands are harder but well encoded, so ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} is sensitive to the articulators carrying lexical content (facial expression is outside the MoAE input; Sec. 8).

4 Three Levels of Conditional Collapse

The ratios decompose SLP failure into three independent levels:

τ1\tau_{1} Initial pose.

Satisfied when the t=0t{=}0 pose varies with the input text (varied); failed when every generated initial pose is identical across sentences (frozen). Visually inspectable in rendered output.

τ2\tau_{2} Output diversity.

Satisfied when outputs vary across inputs as much as GT motions do; failed when outputs cluster around a near-identical mean motion (ρdiv→0\rho_{\mathrm{div}}\to 0).

τ3\tau_{3} Faithfulness.

Satisfied when each output aligns to its specific target and ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} approaches the dataset’s GT-vs-GT reference (Sec. 3.1); failed when alignment is no better than random (ρfaith≈1\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1).

These levels are independently attainable: a model can satisfy τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2} without attaining τ3\tau_{3}. On How2Sign, the checkpoints we rendered show two visual cases. (i) Frozen start ++ jitter trajectory (all three levels collapsed): a near-identical canonical start regardless of input, then small-amplitude noise around the GT marginal mean. This is the dominant failure mode and includes the FID-best checkpoint (row 3 of Tab. 3). (ii) Varied start ++ jitter trajectory (τ1\tau_{1}, τ2\tau_{2} satisfied, τ3\tau_{3} collapsed): a visibly different start per input, but the trajectory is still noise. It appears under aggressive input narrowing (small vocabularies, short sentences). The two full-corpus MDM checkpoints trained with the FK loss (rows 1 and 2 of Tab. 3) satisfy τ2\tau_{2} numerically. Their outputs vary across inputs more than GT motions do (ρdiv≈1.8\rho_{\mathrm{div}}\approx 1.8), yet each output is no closer to its own target than to a random one (ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} 0.960.96 to 0.980.98). (iii) Varied start ++ coherent motion (all satisfied) is never observed on How2Sign; it is reached on the dense-coverage datasets of Sec. 6.

Figure 1 shows the (i)-vs-(ii) contrast directly: rows 1–2 emit a near-identical canonical start regardless of input (τ1\tau_{1} collapsed), row 3 shows visibly different starts (τ1\tau_{1} satisfied). Trajectory slices at five relative times (Fig. S1) show small-amplitude input-independent motion where the corresponding GT rows show coherent gestures — visual τ3\tau_{3} failure even for the strongest τ1\tau_{1}/τ2\tau_{2} checkpoints.

5 Experiments

In all experiments, we refer to “checkpoint” as one fully trained model with distinct design configurations (architecture, conditioning input, dataset subset), trained from scratch and saved at the best epoch.

Datasets. How2Sign [5] is an open-domain English instructional ASL dataset: 3131K training / 2,3572{,}357 test sentences with per-frame SMPL-X [15] parameters; train vocabulary 15,43415{,}434 words. Our default training pool keeps the ∼\sim2626K sentences of 33–3030 words; a checkpoint trained on the unfiltered 3131K set collapses identically (Table S1). Phoenix-2014T [6] is a dataset of German weather broadcasts comprised of 7,0927{,}092 train / 642642 test sentences and SMPL-X fittings from the Signs-as-Tokens release [29]. CSL-Daily [27] is a Chinese daily-life dataset comprised of 18,39918{,}399 train / 1,1761{,}176 test sentences with fittings, from the same release [29]. Each training sentence is performed by 2.82.8 signers on average, and test sentences are unseen. ASL3DWord [4] is a dataset of isolated glosses with 1.21.2K train / 339339 test clips over 103103 gloss types. All four datasets use the same 5353-joint SMPL-X representation, so the diagnostic pipeline remains unchanged.

Conditioning inputs. Next we vary the type of conditioning input and its representation. Sentence: the sentence is encoded into a single pooled token by a frozen contrastive text encoder CLIP-ViT-B/32 [17] for English and German, and the Chinese-CLIP text tower [25] for Chinese (Sec. 6.3). LLM keywords: we prompt an open-source instruction-tuned LLM (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct [16] for English, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct for German and Chinese) to reduce each sentence to a short list of representative content words that will serve as a pseudo-gloss. This keeps the content words (nouns, verbs, pronouns, negation, numerals, meaning-bearing modals), drops function words, and lemmatizes the sentence. The details can be found in Appendix B. A similar LLM extraction is used by Guo et al. [8] for sign language translation. The keywords serve as the closest proxy gloss for How2Sign dataset that does not have gloss annotations; Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily provide native gloss annotations, letting us compare LLM keywords against linguist-annotated gloss. Fused: sentence and keywords are concatenated into a single CLIP input (“sentence ; keywords”). Table 2 shows per language examples of gloss and LLM keywords. Additional examples can be found in Table S2. Note that LLM keywords keep source text order while native gloss follows sign order. All tested checkpoints vary only in the conditioning input.

Models. We evaluate two model families that together cover the recurring design choices in SLP: iterative diffusion and single-pass regression. (i) Diffusion. Our main backbone is MDM [21], a Transformer denoiser that receives the noisy motion sequence together with a timestep token and the frozen CLIP text token, and is trained to predict the noise (architecture in Fig. S2a). It is trained with a per-frame pose MSE on the SMPL-X rotations plus a forward-kinematic term ℒFK\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FK}} that penalizes 33D joint-position error after forward kinematics. One checkpoint (row 3 of Tab. 3) is trained with the pose MSE only; it attains the best FID of all our How2Sign models and is included precisely because FID ranks it first. (ii) Regression. As a deliberately simple non-diffusion baseline we train a clean Transformer-decoder regressor: TT learned frame queries pass through a 66-layer decoder whose cross-attention memory is the single frozen CLIP token, and the network emits the full motion sequence in one forward pass (∼\sim2626M trainable parameters; Fig. S2b). It uses the same pose and FK losses as MDM. Because it is deterministic, ρcond\rho_{\mathrm{cond}} is not defined for it. For all models the architecture, text encoder, and training schedule are held fixed across data and conditioning variants, so differences between rows reflect the data or the conditioning input rather than tuning; hyperparameters are listed in Appendix D.

Evaluation. For each checkpoint we compute (ρcond,ρdiv,ρfaith)(\rho_{\mathrm{cond}},\rho_{\mathrm{div}},\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}) and FID on the full test split, render SMPL-X mesh videos, and visually inspect initial pose and trajectory.

5.1 Main negative result

We trained 1414 sentence-level How2Sign dataset checkpoints spanning two architecture families (diffusion, regression), two conditioning inputs (sentence, LLM keywords), while varying the four characteristics of the dataset: training-set size (1313K/2626K/3131K), vocabulary restriction (top-3,0003{,}000 / top-500500 training vocabulary), utterance length (≤3\leq 3 words; single word), and loss composition. Table 3 shows representative checkpoints. Every How2Sign checkpoint in Tab. 3 attains ρfaith∈[0.95,1.00]\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\in[0.95,1.00], far above its GT-vs-GT reference of 0.8490.849, and no configuration attains τ3\tau_{3}. Holding everything else fixed, growing the training pool from 1313K to 2626K sentences (rows 4–5) worsens ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}} (0.41→0.340.41\to 0.34) while ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays ≈0.95\approx 0.95, inside the collapse range. Note that more data lets the model output the average motion more confidently, yet it does not help the model to respond faithfully to the input. Utterance length (Table S1). Decreasing T=100,50,32T=100,50,32 improves ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}} monotonically (0.45→0.46→0.630.45\to 0.46\to 0.63) leading to shorter sentences satisfying τ2\tau_{2}. So τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2} can be satisfactory by narrowing the input enough (Fig. 1: the top-500500-vocabulary regression checkpoint varies its initial pose), but τ3\tau_{3} cannot.

5.2 The FID and ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} disconnect

Across the 1414 How2Sign checkpoints and our NSA re-implementation (Sec. 7), FID spans from 1.911.91 to 151151 while ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} spans only 0.890.89–1.001.00. The best-FID model (row 3) is the most collapsed (ρfaith=1.00\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=1.00, ρdiv=0.17\rho_{\mathrm{div}}=0.17) and its outputs cluster tightly around the marginal mean, which is exactly what FID rewards. The Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily blocks agree: their lowest FID (1.391.39, 1.341.34) is the regression row, also lowest in ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}}. Hence FID alone does not properly account for text-to-motion alignment. The full table can be found in Table S1.

5.3 BT-BLEU also fails to track faithfulness

We trained a motion-to-text back-translation (BT) model on How2Sign without pretraining. Without pretraining, How2Sign alone does not train a usable translation network. The video translator of Uthus et al. [22] reaches only BLEU-4 ≈1.22\approx 1.22 in this regime. Our BT model reaches BLEU-4 ≈2.5\approx 2.5 even on ground-truth motion, and 1.241.24 on our generated motion. Its translation predictions are often input-independent template language unrelated to the GT sentence (see Tab. 4). The non-zero BLEU score is due to n-gram overlap with high-frequency vocabulary where an autoregressive decoder in the back-translation model is estimating a near-marginal prior. BT-BLEU on How2Sign therefore reflects the weakness of the evaluator more than the quality of the generator. ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} captures this failure directly. BT-BLEU does not.

6 The Coverage Argument

In the following section we present a controlled experiment that sheds light on model collapse when training on How2Sign dataset and performance on the other datasets. We use the same two architectures, frozen text encoder, and diagnostic on four datasets that differ in how densely their training sentences cover the conditions their test sets draw from. Each dataset uses its own MoAE and its own GT-vs-GT reference. The diagnostic ratios are dimensionless and the values are compared across datasets only by band membership, at-reference vs. far-above-reference values.

6.1 Same models, four datasets

The main results on Phoenix-2014T, CSL-Daily, and ASL3DWord are reported in Tab. 3. On How2Sign, both architectures have a ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} gap of 0.100.10–0.130.13 above the 0.8490.849 reference. On Phoenix-2014T both models reach ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} below the 0.8740.874 reference. The generated motion is as close to its target as another human rendition of the same sentence. All four conditioning-string variants stay in that range (Sec. 6.6); Fig. 3a shows a rendered generation against ground truth. CSL-Daily’s reference (0.6730.673) is the strictest of the four, with training sentences performed by 2.82.8 signers on average. Using the Chinese-CLIP text embedding [25] (Sec. 6.3), all five models attain ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} 0.750.75–0.800.80 (Fig. 3b). On gloss-level ASL3DWord the same MDM backbone attains ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} of 0.7310.731 against a 0.7520.752 reference (Fig. 2). The largest corpus (How2Sign, 3131K) is the one that fails its reference, while 4×4\times smaller Phoenix-2014T and 26×26\times smaller ASL3DWord approach their reference. This corroborates the observation that more paired data does not produce faithfulness, and less does not preclude it. It is the structure of the dataset that is the determining factor of the performance.

6.2 Frame-level alignment

In Fig. 3 the generated frames visually track their GT. To check whether this holds beyond selected examples, we measure frame-level agreement directly, complementing the MoAE ratios, which represent each motion as a single embedding vector. We compare motions pose by pose with dynamic time warping (DTW): we convert each motion into per-frame 33D coordinates of the 4444 upper-body joints, align the two sequences in time, and sum the per-frame distances. This sum is divided by the same quantity computed for pairs of unrelated sentences.

We score two kinds of pairs. We take 4040 sentences per dataset that were performed at least twice and score the two human renditions against each other: 0.740.74 on Phoenix-2014T and 0.590.59 on CSL-Daily. Note that the two renditions come from different signers. For the models, we score the generated motion against the GT of the same test sentence (4040 sentences per dataset): 0.860.86 and 0.760.76, farther from the GT than two humans are from each other. Only the most repeated sentences close this gap (Fig. 3a). In short, passing the MoAE test does not yet mean human-level frame-by-frame agreement: our “reaches its reference” claims are about whole sequences (full protocol in Appendix G).

6.3 Model-free evidence: dispersion and retrieval

If the determining factor of collapse is conditional coverage, it should be measurable in the conditioning space itself, with no generator involved. We test this two ways.

Conditioning space dispersion.

On the frozen CLIP text encoder the generators condition on, we measure (a) within-train dispersion: pairwise cosine among training sentences, and (b) coverage: each test sentence’s cosine to its nearest training neighbor (Tab. 5). Phoenix is far denser than How2Sign on every measure. Its 55th-percentile coverage (0.890.89) exceeds How2Sign’s median (0.800.80); mean-centering preserves the gap (0.790.79 vs 0.630.63), and a natively multilingual XLM-R encoder [3] preserves its direction, so the gap is not an artifact of an English encoder reading German.

CSL-Daily is measured on the Chinese-CLIP text tower [25]; its centered coverage (0.710.71) lands between How2Sign (0.630.63) and Phoenix (0.790.79), matching its in-between model results.

Nearest-neighbor retrieval sweep.

For each test sentence, retrieve the nearest training sentence by text embedding and use its GT motion as the prediction — an architecture-free “model” whose faithfulness depends only on coverage (full curves in Appendix F). On How2Sign, ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays flat at ∼\sim0.980.98 as the pool grows from 500500 to 26,00026{,}000 sentences (50×50\times): even the nearest of 2626K training motions is, on average, no closer to a test target than a random one. On Phoenix the same sweep improves with pool size (0.905→0.8670.905\to 0.867), reaching the reference (0.8740.874); on CSL-Daily (Chinese-CLIP) it improves (0.888→0.8680.888\to 0.868) but stays far above the 0.6730.673 reference: test sentences are unseen, so no pool offers a rendition to copy — and every CSL-Daily generator lands below this 0.8680.868 bound (rows 11–15 of Tab. 3), composing beyond retrieval. On How2Sign, more in-domain data adds no coverage, so no model trained on it should be expected to condition — and none does.

6.4 Text encoder effects

Same encoder, opposite outcomes. The same frozen English-pretrained CLIP text encoder reads German on Phoenix-2014T and the model is faithful (ρfaith=0.839\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.839) while encoding English on How2Sign collapses (ρfaith=0.98\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.98). If weak text representations were the primary cause, this ordering would be reversed.
Encoder swap. A more powerful frozen T5-base text encoder [18] in the 2626K How2Sign regression leaves ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} essentially unchanged (0.9540.954 with CLIP, 0.9420.942 with T5).

Text shuffling. On How2Sign’s unfiltered 3131K sentence-MDM checkpoint (row 6 of Table S1), replacing the input sentence moves the output 1.05×1.05\times, no more than re-sampling the noise seed. Word-shuffling leaves faithfulness almost unchanged (0.963→0.9700.963\to 0.970), which suggests that the model output is not affected by conditioning text. This is in contrast to Phoenix-2014T, where sentence replacement moves the output well beyond noise (1.35×1.35\times) while word-shuffling moves it less than a new seed (0.49×0.49\times). ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays near the reference (0.838→0.8550.838\to 0.855): the model reacts to the words themselves, not their order.

6.5 Coverage is necessary, not sufficient

We retrained Progressive Transformers [19], a representative of the autoregressive architecture family on the same clean Phoenix-2014T SMPL-X data. During inference (step counter and output length governed by the model’s own predictions rather than supplied from ground truth), it collapses (ρfaith=0.9999\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.9999; output spread 0.025×0.025\times GT) (see more details in Appendix H).

To conclude: with sparse coverage every architecture we tested collapses, and with dense coverage the architecture and training protocol still decide the outcome. The diagnostic exposes both kinds of failure.

6.6 Conditioning representation

On the dense-coverage corpora we study the effect of the conditioning representation, considering four options, sentence encoding, LLM-extracted keywords (Sec. 5), native gloss (if available in the annotations), and a fused input. Native gloss is the annotation upper bound for the LLM keywords: their gap on annotated corpora measures the proxy’s quality where no annotation exists (How2Sign). On How2Sign, using LLM keywords does not avoid collapse (row 2 of Tab. 3).

On Phoenix, all four alternatives stay at or near the 0.8740.874 reference (rows 6–9): once coverage is dense, no representation choice re-introduces collapse. LLM keywords give the best faithfulness (0.8090.809), matching or exceeding the linguist-annotated gloss (0.8520.852). This is relevant for corpora like How2Sign that do not have gloss annotations. On CSL-Daily (Chinese-CLIP), all four cases share similar range (0.750.75–0.800.80; rows 11–15 of Tab. 3): LLM keywords (0.7870.787) and native gloss (0.7880.788) are indistinguishable, so token order does not decide the outcome, and the fused sentence⊕\oplusgloss input is best (0.7500.750). These differences are small (single runs); the robust conclusion is that no conditioning text turns a collapsing dataset into a healthy one, or the reverse.

7 Discussion

Reproducibility note on Neural Sign Actors.

NSA [1] reports the lowest sentence-level How2Sign FID in the literature but releases neither code nor weights. Following the published description, our re-implementation needed several debugging rounds to converge; our best run reaches FID ≈151\approx 151 with ρfaith≈1.00\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1.00 and no input-specific motion in rendered samples. We do not interpret this discrepancy; it does not affect our claim, since even an NSA-class FID is consistent with τ1\tau_{1}/τ2\tau_{2} satisfied ++ τ3\tau_{3} collapsed. That is the best regime any of our How2Sign checkpoints reaches. We read prior FID gains in this line as improvements in τ1\tau_{1} and partial τ2\tau_{2}, not τ3\tau_{3}.

Reported successes on Phoenix and CSL-Daily.

Qualitatively convincing generation is reported on Phoenix-2014T [19, 10, 24, 26] and CSL-Daily [29, 28]; that evidence is structurally consistent with our frame-level analysis. The displayed sentences concentrate on the densest conditions — Progressive Transformers leads with the canonical broadcast opener, three of SOKE’s four Phoenix examples are broadcast greetings — precisely the conditions our DTW analysis places inside the human band for our models as well (Sec. 6.2). Every figure shows one GT rendition and no human–human baseline, in formats that hide frame-level error, and no verifiable generator weights were obtainable. Whether any attains human-band frame alignment is thus open — and directly testable with our released MoAE, references, and DTW protocol. This is not a claim that these systems fail; it supplies the missing calibration.

Recommended evaluation protocol.

SLP papers should report (ρcond,ρdiv,ρfaith)(\rho_{\mathrm{cond}},\rho_{\mathrm{div}},\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}) alongside FID and BT-BLEU, judging ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} against the dataset’s GT-vs-GT reference (Eq. 9) on a shared released MoAE, and, where same-sentence GT pairs exist, frame-level DTW alignability against the human–human baseline (Sec. 6.2). ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} is a necessary-condition check: passing it does not certify linguistic adequacy, which requires native-signer evaluation.

What would fix How2Sign?

Within-corpus scaling does not add coverage (Sec. 6.3), so the candidates are external: large-scale text-to-motion pretraining, transfer from dense-coverage corpora, or word-level supervision injected from outside the paired corpus — the route SOKE’s dictionary retrieval takes [29], consistent with the coverage account. The sign-to-text direction points the same way: a translator trained directly on How2Sign reaches only BLEU-4 ≈1.22\approx 1.22, with faithful translation emerging only after 1111K hours of pretraining [22]. None is evaluated under our diagnostic here; pretraining remains plausible but undemonstrated.

Societal impact.

SLP evaluation rigor directly affects Deaf and hard-of-hearing users: metrics that reward text-independent motion can promote systems producing fluent-looking but meaningless signing. A diagnostic calibrated against real signers’ renditions is a prerequisite for trustworthy progress claims in accessibility.

8 Conclusion

We introduced a training-free diagnostic that exposes conditional collapse in sentence-level SLP, judged against per-dataset GT-vs-GT references, and showed that (i) 1414 How2Sign checkpoints across two architecture families never attain faithfulness while FID varies ∼\sim80×80\times uncorrelated with it, and (ii) the driver is per-condition coverage: the same architectures reach their sequence-level references on densely-covered Phoenix-2014T and ASL3DWord with less paired data, condition partially on CSL-Daily, and collapse on How2Sign at every available scale. A frame-level DTW lens calibrated on human–human consistency is stricter still: even at-reference Phoenix reaches the human band only on its densest formulaic conditions. Coverage is necessary but not sufficient — Progressive Transformers collapses on dense Phoenix — so the diagnostic separates data-limited from architecture-limited failure. We release the MoAE checkpoints and diagnostic code under permissive licenses.

Limitations.

Our checkpoints do not cover the full design space; large-scale text-to-motion pretraining remains untested. The MoAE omits facial expression and non-manual markers, and hands are reconstructed less precisely than body (nRMSE\mathrm{nRMSE} 0.300.30–0.370.37 vs 0.170.17–0.200.20): ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} is a necessary-condition check on manual articulation, not a certificate of linguistic adequacy. Correlating the diagnostic with native-signer judgment is the key next step.

A Full How2Sign results

Table S1 reports all 1414 sentence-level How2Sign checkpoints (rows 1–14), the How2Sign GT-vs-GT reference (row 15), and the gloss-level ASL3DWord checkpoint (row 16). Rows 1–5 and 16 of Table 3 are rows 1, 2, 5, 7, 8, and 16 of this table.

Input modality

(sent / keywords). Sentence: the raw English How2Sign sentence, encoded by frozen CLIP-ViT-B/32 [17]. LLM keywords: we prompt an open-source LLM to extract pseudo-glosses (short ordered lists of base-form content words) from sentences; the exact prompt, model, and representative outputs are in Sec. B. ASL gloss annotations are unavailable for How2Sign, so the LLM keywords serve as the closest available proxy.

Training subset.

The unfiltered How2Sign release has 3131K training sentences. Our default training pool is the ∼\sim2626K subset obtained by a 33-to-3030 word sentence-length filter that removes long-tail outliers; rows 1–5 and rows 8–14 of Tab. S1 use this 2626K pool. As an end-to-end check that the filter is not load-bearing, we also trained an identical MDM+sentence variant on the unfiltered 3131K-sentence release (row 6): ρfaith=0.98\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.98 matches the 2626K run exactly, and the other diagnostic ratios fall in the same band. Beyond these two, we evaluate a 1313K random subsample of the 2626K pool (row 7) and two families of input-narrowing variants: vocabulary-restricted (K=K): sentences whose words all fall within the top-KK most-frequent training vocabulary (K=3000, K=500); and short-sentence: short1 (single-word) or short3 (≤3\leq 3-word) sentences drawn from the full 3131K-sentence release (these bypass the 33-to-3030 word filter by design). Exact train/test counts are in Sec. D. Row labels combine the two axes (e.g. K=500 keywords). Each filter is applied to the raw English sentence regardless of encoder input, so corresponding sent and keywords rows use identical training and test sentences and differ only in what the encoder sees.

Training and evaluation.

Within each model family, the same training settings are used across all data variants: batch size 256256, learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, and 100100 epochs for sentence-length variants; batch size 6464 and 200200 epochs for short-sentence variants. For each checkpoint we compute (ρcond,ρdiv,ρfaith)(\rho_{\mathrm{cond}},\rho_{\mathrm{div}},\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}) and FID on the full test split. When training was vocabulary-restricted, we evaluate on the matching test subset (the test sentences whose words also pass the filter). We additionally render generated motions as SMPL-X mesh videos and visually inspect them for τ1\tau_{1} and trajectory coherence.

One axis at a time.

Holding everything else fixed: quantity (rows 7 vs 8): 1313K →\to 2626K worsens ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}} (0.41→0.340.41\to 0.34); ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays in the collapse band (both ≈0.95\approx 0.95). More data lets the model output the average motion more confidently; it does not teach the model to respond to the input. Vocabulary restriction (rows 8, 9, 10): shrinking the training vocabulary from 15,43415{,}434 to 3,0003{,}000 and 500500 types leaves ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} at 0.950.95–0.970.97; only the initial pose becomes varied at K=500K{=}500 (V+J). Utterance length (rows 10, 13, 14): T=100,50,32T=100,50,32 improves ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}} monotonically (0.45→0.46→0.630.45\to 0.46\to 0.63); shorter sentences satisfy τ2\tau_{2}. Backbone (rows 1–4): the multi-scale MSTrans denoiser (Sec. D) changes FID by <0.2<0.2 and ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} by ≤0.02\leq 0.02. So τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2} can be satisfied by narrowing the input enough, but τ3\tau_{3} cannot: changing data quantity, vocabulary density, sequence length, or backbone all leave ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} far above the 0.8490.849 reference.

FID range.

Across rows 1–14 plus our Neural Sign Actors re-implementation (Sec. 7; FID ≈151\approx 151, the upper end), FID spans 1.911.91 to 151151 while ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} spans only 0.890.89 to 1.001.00; the Pearson correlation between them is near zero.

Gloss-level ASL3DWord (row 16).

We apply the exact same MDM backbone, loss, and diagnostic pipeline to ASL3DWord [4] (WLASL-101 SMPL-X subset, 1.21.2K train / 339339 test / 103103 glosses, T=60T{=}60), where the task is one English gloss →\to one isolated sign. Row 16 reports ρcond=4.80\rho_{\mathrm{cond}}=4.80, ρdiv=1.14\rho_{\mathrm{div}}=1.14, ρfaith=0.73\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 on the full test split; ρfaith=0.73\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 matches the ASL3DWord GT-vs-GT same-gloss reference ρfaith,ref=0.752\rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}}=0.752 (Sec. E). WLASL records each word with multiple signers, and the same word performed by different signers varies substantially in hand shape and motion, so even a perfect generator that copies a real recording of the target word cannot score below this within-word across-signer reference; the checkpoint lands right at it (renders in Fig. 2). This positive example is not a new word-level SLP method; it confirms that the diagnostic tells working models apart from collapsed ones.

B LLM keyword extraction

The LLM keywords conditioning input (Sec. 5) is produced by prompting an open-source instruction-tuned LLM to reduce each sentence to a short ordered list of base-form content words (a pseudo-gloss). For English (How2Sign) we use Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct [16] with greedy decoding and max_new_tokens =256=256; for German (Phoenix-2014T) and Chinese (CSL-Daily) we use Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with greedy decoding and max_new_tokens =96=96. No system message is used beyond the prompt itself. Keywords are extracted once per sentence and cached; every training variant of a corpus reads the same cache, so the sentence, keyword, and fused variants of one corpus train on the identical sample set (the length filter is always computed on the original sentence). The prompts share one three-step recipe (phrase-level chunking →\to keep/drop decision →\to citation form), adapted per language: the German prompt handles auxiliary chains, separable/particle verbs, and case inflection; the Chinese prompt handles aspect particles, measure words, and the

把/被constructions, and requires standard word segmentation. All three prompts instruct the model to keep source order; the prompts are reproduced below with instructions verbatim and the few-shot example lists abridged to four per language.

Representative outputs.

Table S2 shows uncurated examples in the three languages next to the corpus’s native gloss where one exists. The extractor is imperfect: occasional artefacts include over-eager merging of adjacent tokens and sporadic lemmatisation slips. These are systematic but rare and do not change the conditioning regime: on How2Sign no keyword variant escapes collapse, and on Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily the keyword variants stay in the same band as the sentence and native-gloss variants (Table 3).

Fused input.

The fused variant concatenates the sentence and its keywords (Phoenix-2014T) or native gloss (CSL-Daily) into one string, “sentence ; keywords”, which is then encoded by the same frozen text encoder as a single pooled token. Nothing else changes.

English prompt.

The prompt below is sent to the LLM once per sentence, with {input_sentence} replaced by the source text and the model’s output read as the keyword string. Arrows in the original prompt files are rendered as -> here.

You are an ASL (American Sign Language) linguistic expert. Your task is to extract pseudo-gloss from an English sentence.

Pseudo-gloss is a sequence of words that determine the core meaning of the sentence. Each word should correspond to a distinct sign that an ASL signer would produce. The test is: ’’If I remove this word, does the core meaning of the sentence change?’’

Follow these three steps in order:

## Step 1: Phrase-level chunking

Identify multi-word structures and treat them as a single unit BEFORE analyzing individual words:

- Auxiliary verb chains: ’’is going to’’, ’’has been doing’’, ’’would have been’’, ’’are going to be learning’’ -> mark the entire chain as auxiliary, drop it all

- Phrasal verbs: ’’get out’’, ’’pick up’’, ’’break down’’, ’’set up’’, ’’hold down’’ -> mark as a single verb unit, keep the particle

- Light verb constructions: ’’make sure’’->’’sure’’, ’’take a look’’->’’look’’, ’’get rid of’’->’’rid’’ — the light verb (make/take/get) is structural, drop it

- Discourse frames: ’’let me/let’s’’ (when meaning ’’allow me to’’), ’’you know’’, ’’I mean’’ -> drop

This step is critical: without it, ’’going’’ inside ’’is going to’’ would be mistakenly kept as ’’go’’.

## Step 2: Decide which units determine the core meaning

Keep words that would be produced as an independent sign in ASL:

- Content words: nouns, verbs, adjectives, content adverbs (always, sometimes, often)

- Pronouns: i, you, we, he, she, they, me, my, your, his, her, our, their

- Negation: not, no, never, nothing, none, nobody

- Interrogative WH-words: what, when, where, who, why, how, which (in questions)

- Numbers: one, two, three, second, third, etc.

- Modal verbs that carry meaning: can (ability), might/maybe (possibility), should/must (obligation)

- Spatial/directional words when they express location or movement: inside, outside, up, down, around, forward, back, off, over

Drop words that don’t change the core meaning:

- Articles: a, an, the

- Copulas: is, am, are, was, were (as linking verb)

- Auxiliary chains identified in Step 1

- Conjunctions: and, but, or, so, because, if, that, then

- Structural prepositions: of, to (infinitive marker), at, by, for, with, from (when purely grammatical)

- Degree modifiers: very, really, pretty (as ’’fairly’’), quite, extremely, a lot — these are expressed through sign intensity in ASL, not as separate signs

- Discourse fillers: okay, well, actually, basically, just, literally, essentially

- Determiners: this, that, these, those, any, some (when not carrying meaning)

- Relative pronouns: which/that introducing a clause (’’the button, which opens...’’ -> drop ’’which’’)

- Structural ’’how’’: ’’learn how to play’’ -> drop ’’how’’ (vs interrogative ’’How do you play?’’ -> keep ’’how’’)

If the same content repeats for emphasis in the original sentence, keep it only once (de-duplicate).

## Step 3: Restore to citation form

Lemmatize each kept word to its base/dictionary form:

- Verb tense: gives->give, went->go, tied->tie, learning->learn, spoken->speak

- Plural: steps->step, hands->hand, feet->foot, children->child

- Comparative/superlative: highest->high, bigger->big, better->good

- Never produce a non-word fragment (e.g. other->oth is WRONG, keep ’’other’’)

## Output format

Output ONLY the pseudo-gloss as a single line of space-separated lowercase words. No explanation.

## Examples

Sentence: I’m having fun.

Gloss: i fun

Sentence: You don’t have to take big steps.

Gloss: you not take big step

Sentence: Hold down the second string on the fourth fret and then pluck the second and third string.

Gloss: hold down second string fourth fret pluck second third string

Sentence: Today we’re going to be learning how to play Portal, a game by Valve Software.

Gloss: today we learn play portal game valve software

German prompt.

You are a DGS (German Sign Language / Deutsche Gebärdensprache) linguistic expert. Your task is to extract pseudo-gloss from a German sentence.

Pseudo-gloss is a sequence of words that determine the core meaning of the sentence. Each word should correspond to a distinct sign that a DGS signer would produce. The test is: ’’If I remove this word, does the core meaning of the sentence change?’’

Follow these three steps in order:

## Step 1: Phrase-level chunking

Identify multi-word structures and treat them as a single unit BEFORE analyzing individual words:

- Auxiliary chains: ’’ist gegangen’’, ’’hat gemacht’’, ’’wird kommen’’, ’’war gewesen’’, ’’sind worden’’ -> mark the entire chain as auxiliary, drop the auxiliary (sein/haben/werden), keep only the participle/infinitive lemma

- Modal + infinitive: ’’kann gehen’’, ’’muss machen’’, ’’soll bleiben’’ -> keep the modal only if it carries meaning (kann=ability, muss=obligation), keep the main verb

- Reflexive constructions: ’’sich freuen’’, ’’sich ärgern’’ -> drop ’’sich’’ (reflexive marker), keep the verb

- Particle verbs: ’’aufstehen’’, ’’ankommen’’, ’’wegfahren’’ -> keep as one unit (already a single lemma)

- Light verb constructions: ’’Bescheid geben’’->’’geben/inform’’, ’’in Verbindung treten’’->’’verbinden’’ — collapse to a single content word

- Discourse frames: ’’und nun’’, ’’weiß ich nicht’’, ’’denke ich’’ -> drop the frame, keep the proposition

## Step 2: Decide which units determine the core meaning

Keep words that would be produced as an independent sign in DGS:

- Content words: nouns (Wetter, Regen), verbs (gehen, regnen, sein-as-existence), adjectives (warm, kalt), content adverbs (heute, morgen, oft)

- Pronouns: ich, du, er, sie, wir, ihr, mein, dein, sein, unser — DGS expresses these via IX (indexing) and POSS signs

- Negations: nicht, nie, niemals, kein, keine, nichts, niemand, weder, ohne

- Interrogative WH-words: was, wann, wo, wer, warum, wie, welcher

- Numbers and quantifiers: ein/eine (when meaning ’’one’’, not as article), zwei, drei, viele, wenige, alle

- Modal verbs that carry meaning: kann (ability), muss/soll (obligation), darf (permission), will (desire)

- Spatial/directional words: oben, unten, hier, dort, vor, hinter, rechts, links — when expressing location

- Time expressions: heute, morgen, gestern, jetzt, bald, früh, spät

Drop words that don’t change the core meaning:

- Articles: der, die, das, den, dem, des, ein, eine, einen, einer, eines (when used as articles, not numerals)

- Copulas / structural sein: ist, sind, war, waren, sei, gewesen — when linking (’’ist warm’’ -> just ’’warm’’)

- Auxiliary chains identified in Step 1: haben + Partizip, werden + Infinitiv (future)

- Conjunctions: und, oder, aber, denn, weil, dass, obwohl, wenn, falls, sondern

- Structural prepositions: in, auf, an, von, mit, für, bei, zu, nach (when grammatical/structural)

- Degree modifiers: sehr, ziemlich, ganz, recht, durchaus — DGS expresses degree via sign intensity, not separate signs

- Discourse fillers: also, eigentlich, halt, eben, mal, doch, ja, schon, nun

- Vague quantifiers / particles: etwas, irgendwie, sozusagen

- Impersonal ’’es’’: ’’es regnet’’ -> just ’’regnen’’; ’’es gibt’’ -> ’’geben/exist’’

- Filler relative pronouns: der/die/das as relative pronouns introducing subordinate clauses

If the same content repeats for emphasis in the original sentence, keep it only once (de-duplicate).

## Step 3: Restore to citation form (German lemmatization)

Lemmatize each kept word to its base/dictionary form:

- Verb conjugation: gehe/gehst/geht/gingen->gehen; regnet/regnete->regnen; bin/bist/ist/war->sein

- Plural: Tagen->Tag; Wolken->Wolke; Häuser->Haus; Männer->Mann

- Adjective inflection: tiefer/tiefen/tieferes->tief; kräftige/kräftigen->kräftig; nächsten->nächst

- Comparative/superlative: höher->hoch; größer->groß; am besten->gut

- Decapitalize all words. DGS gloss is conventionally upper-case, but for our pipeline we output lowercase for tokenizer compatibility.

## Output format

Output ONLY the pseudo-gloss as a single line of space-separated lowercase words. No explanation. No quotation marks. No leading punctuation.

## Examples

Sentence: ich freue mich.

Gloss: ich freuen

Sentence: und nun die wettervorhersage für morgen donnerstag den zwölften august

Gloss: wettervorhersage morgen donnerstag zwölft august

Gloss: nordwesten bleiben heute nacht trocken muss kräftig schauer rechnen

Chinese prompt.

Note that the few-shot sentences of this prompt are deliberately not used as examples anywhere in the paper.

You are a CSL (Chinese Sign Language / 中国手语) linguistic expert. Your task is to extract keywords (pseudo-gloss) from a Chinese sentence.

Keywords are a sequence of words that determine the core meaning of the sentence. Each word should correspond to a distinct sign that a CSL signer would produce. The test is: ’’If I remove this word, does the core meaning of the sentence change?’’ Keep the words in the ORIGINAL sentence order.

Follow these three steps in order:

## Step 1: Phrase-level chunking

Identify multi-word structures and treat them as a single unit BEFORE analyzing individual characters:

- Fixed expressions: 对不起, 没关系, 不客气, 谢谢, 再见 -> keep as ONE unit, do not split

- Light verb constructions: ’’打手语’’->’’手语’’ (打 is structural), ’’叫什么名字’’->’’什么 名字’’ (叫 is structural), ’’取名字’’->keep the action verb 取 and 名字

- Aspect/structural particles attached to verbs: 了, 着, 过 -> drop the particle, keep the verb

- ’’是……的’’ emphasis frame -> drop 是 and 的, keep the content inside

- 把/被 constructions -> drop the marker 把/被, keep agent, patient, and verb

## Step 2: Decide which units determine the core meaning

Keep words that would be produced as an independent sign in CSL:

- Content words: nouns (房间, 名字, 工作), verbs (去, 认识, 介绍, 起床), adjectives (好, 小, 高兴)

- Pronouns: 我, 你, 他, 她, 我们, 你们, 他们, 这, 那 (when referring to a thing/place)

- Negation: 不, 没, 没有, 别, 从不

- Question words: 什么, 谁, 哪, 哪里, 几, 多少, 为什么, 怎么

- Numbers: 一, 二, 三, 十, 五十, 100 — keep the numeral, DROP the measure word after it (个, 只, 条, 本, 张, 位, 岁 keep 岁 only when age is the point of the sentence)

- Modal verbs that carry meaning: 会 (ability), 能/可以 (possibility/permission), 要/想 (desire), 应该/必须 (obligation)

- Time words: 今天, 明天, 昨天, 今年, 现在, 每天, 早上, 晚上

- Location/direction words when they express real location: 上, 下, 里, 外, 前, 后, 旁边, 家

Drop words that don’t change the core meaning:

- Structural particles: 的, 地, 得

- Aspect/sentence-final particles: 了, 着, 过, 吗, 呢, 吧, 啊, 呀

- Copula 是 when it just links (’’他是老师’’ -> 他 老师)

- Existence verb 有 when a number already carries the meaning (’’我家有三个人’’ -> 我 家 三 人)

- Measure words / classifiers: 个, 只, 条, 本, 张, 位, 件, 辆

- Conjunctions: 和, 跟, 或者, 但是, 因为, 所以, 如果, 虽然, 然后

- Structural prepositions: 在, 从, 到, 对, 给, 向, 跟 (when purely grammatical; keep when they express real location or destination)

- Degree adverbs: 很, 非常, 太, 特别, 真, 挺 — CSL expresses degree through sign intensity, not separate signs

- Discourse fillers and adverbs of emphasis: 就, 都, 也, 还, 又, 再, 其实, 当然

If the same content repeats for emphasis, keep it only once (de-duplicate).

## Step 3: Output as segmented words

Chinese has no inflection, so no lemmatization is needed. Segment the kept content into standard Chinese words (not single characters unless the word is one character). Keep the original sentence order.

## Output format

Output ONLY the keywords as a single line of space-separated Chinese words. No explanation. No quotation marks. No punctuation.

Keywords: 你 什么 名字

Keywords: 我 家 三 人
