C Back-translation evaluator: training details and failure modes

Training setup.

Our back-translation (motion-to-text) evaluator on How2Sign is trained pose-to-text with translation cross-entropy only, no gloss-CTC loss, no pretrained CSLR features, no auxiliary pretraining. Input is axis-angle SMPL-X; decoding at evaluation is beam-55; the test split has n=2,357n=2{,}357 paired sentences. In this regime BT-BLEU-4 plateaus at a ceiling of ≈2.5\approx 2.5 even on GT motion. Without pretraining, How2Sign alone does not train a usable translation network, and cross-regime comparisons against gloss-CTC-supervised evaluators (e.g. Sign Language Transformers [2]) are not directly meaningful.

Failure-mode commentary.

Table 4 shows 33 representative GT/prediction pairs for our generated motion (BLEU-4 =1.24=1.24). The no-pretraining video translator of Uthus et al. [22] reaches a similar BLEU-4 ≈1.22\approx 1.22. The pattern is consistent across the test split: (i) input-independent high-frequency template language — instructional constructions (“you can do it”, “you want to make sure”, “i’m going to take my right/left hand”) and pronoun-heavy filler — whose semantic content is unrelated to the GT motion; and (ii) degenerate end-of-sequence repetition (“very light, very light, very light, …\ldots”). Both patterns are characteristic of an autoregressive decoder estimating a near-marginal language-model prior with negligible conditional signal from the encoded motion. A non-zero BLEU score arises from short n-gram overlap with How2Sign’s high-frequency vocabulary, not from recovered text content; the diagnostic counterpart, ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}, captures this failure directly.

D Implementation details

MoAE.

The MoAE ϕ\phi of the diagnostic is a small transformer autoencoder operating on per-frame 33-D joint coordinates: each SMPL-X axis-angle sequence is first lifted to T×144×3T\times 144\times 3 joints by SMPL-X forward kinematics, restricted to the 4444 upper-body joints (spine, head, shoulders, elbows, wrists, all 3030 finger joints), and made pelvis-relative, yielding per-frame input dimension D=132D=132. A linear projection lifts each frame to a dmodel=256d_{\mathrm{model}}=256 token; learnable absolute positional embeddings are added; a 33-layer transformer encoder (44 attention heads, feed-forward dim 512512, GELU, pre-LN) produces contextualized per-frame features. A masked mean over valid frames (padding excluded) gives the 256256-dim bottleneck zz. The decoder broadcasts zz across the target sequence length, adds the same positional embeddings, runs through another 33-layer transformer stack with the same hyper-parameters, and projects back to DD. Position embeddings are shared between encoder and decoder; padding is handled with a boolean mask in both directions.

Training loss. For each batch we minimize per-frame MSE between reconstruction and target plus an αvel=0.5\alpha_{\mathrm{vel}}=0.5 MSE on the first-difference (velocity) of the reconstruction:

ℒMoAE=MSE⁡(x^,x)+αvel​MSE​(Δ​x^,Δ​x).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MoAE}}\;=\;\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{x},x)\;+\;\alpha_{\mathrm{vel}}\,\mathrm{MSE}(\Delta\hat{x},\Delta x).

The velocity term is essential: without it, the MoAE collapses to emitting a per-sample mean pose at every frame, which would make zz insensitive to motion dynamics and defeat the diagnostic; the encoder must retain information about how the body moves, not only what poses it visits. Training: the target dataset’s train motions only, sequence length T=200T=200 frames, batch size 128128, 100100 epochs, AdamW [14] at lr 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, dropout 0.10.1 (eval at dropout 00), bf16 mixed precision. The encoder is never exposed to model-generated motion during training, so the bottleneck does not learn collapse-specific features that could bias the diagnostic toward any particular generator. The diagnostic has the limitations of any MoAE: a poorly-trained MoAE could in principle push ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} artificially close to 11. We address this with a single frozen MoAE trained on the target dataset’s GT train motions, the MoAE-initialization and GT-vs-GT checks of Sec. 3.2, and an independent check against visual classification of rendered outputs, which gives the same conclusion on every checkpoint where we did it. One MoAE of this architecture and recipe is trained per dataset (How2Sign, Phoenix-2014T, CSL-Daily, ASL3DWord), and the same frozen checkpoint scores every diagnostic on that dataset, removing per-paper feature inconsistency. A further MoAE of the same architecture, trained on Phoenix-2014T MediaPipe keypoints (7,0967{,}096 sequences), is used only for the PT experiment of Sec. H.

Cross-dataset ratios are qualitative, not quantitative.

The ratios ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}}, ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}, ρcond\rho_{\mathrm{cond}} are dimensionless within one ϕ\phi: numerator and denominator are L2 distances in the same latent space, so the random-pairing baseline cancels the absolute scale. Therefore, within a single dataset, an ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} of 0.730.73 vs 0.960.96 means the model is genuinely more faithful, not that one ϕ\phi was “stricter”. Across datasets, however, the latent geometries differ and the same numerical ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} value need not correspond to identical motion quality. We use cross-dataset comparisons qualitatively only, to argue band membership relative to each dataset’s own GT-vs-GT reference (Sec. E): ASL3DWord 0.730.73 against its reference of 0.7520.752; Phoenix-2014T 0.810.81–0.850.85 against 0.8740.874; CSL-Daily 0.750.75–0.800.80 against 0.6730.673; How2Sign 0.890.89–1.001.00 against 0.8490.849 — never as an ordinal ranking of two distinct-dataset checkpoints by raw ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}.

ASL3DWord MoAE calibration.

The diffusion checkpoint’s ρfaith=0.73\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 on gloss-level ASL3DWord (row 16 of Tab. S1) is interpreted against the within-ASL3DWord GT-vs-GT reference: 339339 test motions are encoded by the same ASL3DWord MoAE used elsewhere; pairwise L2 distances in the latent are partitioned into same-gloss pairs (874874 pairs, both encodings GT clips of the same target gloss) and different-gloss pairs (113,708113{,}708). The same-gloss mean distance (0.8260.826) divided by the different-gloss mean distance (1.0981.098) gives ρfaith,ref=0.752\rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}}=0.752, the lowest ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} achievable on this MoAE under perfect within-class generation. The checkpoint’s 0.730.73 is 0.0220.022 below this value, meaning generated motion is, in the MoAE latent, on average as close to its target as a second GT clip of the same gloss. Consequently the gap between ASL3DWord (0.730.73) and the How2Sign band ([0.89,1.00][0.89,1.00]) understates the actual difference: How2Sign checkpoints sit 0.040.04–0.150.15 above their 0.8490.849 reference, ASL3DWord is at its reference.

Data preparation for Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily.

Both corpora use the per-frame SMPL-X fittings released with Signs as Tokens [29], aggregated per video into axis-angle sequences with the same layout as How2Sign (5353 joints × 3\times\,3). Global orientation is zeroed for both GT and generated motions before encoding (the generators are root-normalized). Sequences are resampled to T=100T=100 frames by uniform index sampling. The same 33-to-3030 length filter as How2Sign is applied to the original sentence (words for German, characters for Chinese), never to the keyword or gloss string, giving 7,0037{,}003 train / 641641 test sentences on Phoenix-2014T and 18,39918{,}399 train / 1,1761{,}176 test on CSL-Daily; every conditioning variant of a corpus therefore trains and is evaluated on the identical sample set. Phoenix sentences are the German translation field and native gloss is the orth field of the corpus annotation (∼\sim1,0661{,}066 DGS gloss types over ∼\sim77K sentence–motion pairs, against ∼\sim1515K English word types over ∼\sim3131K pairs on How2Sign); CSL-Daily sentences and gloss are the dataset’s own annotations.

Diffusion variants.

Figure S2 draws the three networks used throughout the paper: the MDM denoiser (a), the clean regression model (b), and the MoAE (c). The diffusion experiments cover 22 backbones and 22–44 conditioning strings (plus a phonology-augmented variant), all on a standard MDM [21] base (Fig. S2a: 44-layer Transformer encoder, d=512d{=}512, 88 heads, timestep and condition tokens prepended, ϵ\epsilon-prediction). For every component below the finding on How2Sign is the same: ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} remains in the marginal-collapse band [0.89,1.00][0.89,1.00] regardless of which combination is used.

Backbones (2). Standard: the MDM denoiser of Fig. S2a. Multi-scale temporal transformer (MSTrans): the same denoiser with the encoder replaced by a 44-scale temporal encoder at frame-rate factors 1,2,4,81,2,4,8 with cross-scale fusion, intended to capture multi-rate motion structure (slow trajectory ++ fast hand articulation): the noisy motion is processed at strides 1,2,4,81,2,4,8 by four independent Transformer encoders, each cross-attending to the text token, and the per-scale features are upsampled to TT frames and fused. It changes FID by <0.2<0.2 and ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} by ≤0.02\leq 0.02 (Tab. S1, rows 3–4).

Conditioning inputs. Raw sentence, encoded by the frozen text encoder and pooled to a single token; LLM keywords (Sec. B); on the gloss-annotated corpora also native gloss and the fused string. The text encoder is CLIP-ViT-B/32 [17] for English and German and the Chinese-CLIP text tower [25] for Chinese, using its CLS token after the contrastive projection (mean-pooled hidden states form a new anisotropic cone and are not used). On How2Sign we additionally tested a phonology-augmented keyword input with per-token phonological-attribute embeddings following Hong and Kosecka [9]; its collapse pattern is unchanged and it is not separately tabulated.

Loss and sampling. Per-frame pose MSE plus an FK joint-position MSE term. All MDM variants are trained with classifier-free guidance (10%10\% condition dropout) and sampled with guidance scale 3.03.0; the Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily runs use T=100T=100, batch size 6464, and 100100 epochs, identical across the sentence, keyword, gloss, and fused variants of a corpus.

Clean regression model.

The clean regression model is a 66-layer Transformer decoder [23] with D=512D=512, 88 heads, 0.10.1 dropout, GELU. The decoder’s queries are TT learnable positional embeddings; cross-attention memory is a single text token from the frozen text encoder. The output projects to 132132 upper-body axis-angle dimensions. Training: AdamW (β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999), weight decay 10−210^{-2}), OneCycleLR schedule with 5%5\% warmup and cosine annealing, fp16 mixed precision. Loss is ℒpose+λFK​ℒFK\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pose}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FK}} (per-frame pose MSE and FK joint-position MSE) with λFK=5\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}=5. Total trainable parameters ∼\sim2626M (with frozen text encoder excluded). Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily regression runs use batch size 6464, lr 10−410^{-4}, and 100100 / 6565 epochs respectively (the CSL-Daily evaluation loss plateaus from epoch ∼\sim7070; the reported checkpoint is the best-validation one).

Differences from Progressive Transformers (PT).

The clean regression model differs from PT [19] in four ways: (i) we generate all TT frames in a single forward pass, whereas PT is autoregressive (one frame at a time); (ii) output length TT is fixed per sample, whereas PT uses a learned step counter to decide when to stop, which the released protocol drives with GT timing at inference (Sec. H); (iii) the text encoder is frozen CLIP (a single pooled token), whereas PT trains its own text encoder over T5-style tokenization; (iv) the decoder sees only the text embedding via cross-attention, with no feedback from previously generated frames. These simplifications remove any dependence on GT timing at inference and let the row report what a basic Transformer-decoder ++ text cross-attention recipe achieves at the same paired-data budget.

Vocabulary-restricted training subsets.

The K=3000K{=}3000 and K=500K{=}500 whitelists, as well as the ≤1\leq 1-word and ≤3\leq 3-word short-sentence whitelists, are derived from frequencies on How2Sign train. The K=KK{=}K filter keeps only sentences whose words are all within the top-KK most-frequent training-vocabulary words. The whitelist is always defined on the raw-sentence vocabulary regardless of whether the model receives the sentence or the LLM keywords as input; the sent and keywords variants in Tab. S1 therefore share the same set of training and test sentences and differ only in the conditioning modality. For each variant we store the train and test sentence lists under the same train-frequency vocab, ensuring within-distribution evaluation. Counts (train / test): K=3000K{=}3000: 13,571/89013{,}571/890; K=500K{=}500: 2,918/2412{,}918/241; ≤3\leq 3-word: 1,502/1211{,}502/121; ≤1\leq 1-word: 564/44564/44.

E Per-dataset GT-vs-GT reference protocol

Eq. (9) defines ρfaith,ref\rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} as the mean latent distance between two GT renditions of the same text divided by the mean latent distance between renditions of different texts. All references use the dataset’s own frozen MoAE, the same root-zeroing and T=100T=100 resampling as the diagnostic, and pairs drawn exactly as for the generator (numerator and denominator on the same rendition pool). Table 1 lists the group and pair counts; the mean latent distances (same-text / different-text pairs) behind each value are ASL3DWord 0.826/1.0980.826/1.098, Phoenix-2014T 2.167/2.4792.167/2.479, CSL-Daily 1.236/1.8361.236/1.836, How2Sign 3.346/3.9403.346/3.940 (all cross-video repeats: 5.230/5.2485.230/5.248).

ASL3DWord.

Groups are glosses; 100100 of the 103103 test glosses have ≥2\geq 2 clips (different signers). Same-gloss pairs are across signers by construction.

Phoenix-2014T.

Groups are exact German sentences recurring with ≥2\geq 2 renditions in the pooled train++test split (dev excluded); 5050 such sentences exist, mostly formulaic broadcast openers and closers. Many renditions share a signer, which makes the reference conservative (same-signer pairs are closer than cross-signer pairs, lowering ρfaith,ref\rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} and making it harder to reach).

CSL-Daily.

Every training sentence is re-performed by several signers (2.82.8 on average, up to 66), so same-text groups are abundant (∼\sim6.56.5K); we sample 1,0001{,}000 groups (seed fixed) from the pooled train++test split, dev excluded. 99.6%99.6\% of same-sentence pairs are cross-signer (only 99 of 2,5042{,}504 share a signer): the CSL reference measures scripted cross-signer consistency, the strictest of the four.

How2Sign.

Pooled train++test contains 789789 exact-repeat groups (2,3382{,}338 renditions), but most are within-video: re-alignment overlaps, duplicated metadata rows, or same-take repeats (e.g. exercise counting), which carry no independent rendition. Restricting to repeats across distinct videos leaves 181181 groups (923923 renditions), dominated by one- and two-word greetings and fillers (“Hi!”, “Okay?”, “Cheers!”) whose clips carry no sentence-specific motion: same-text pairs are as far apart as random pairs and the reference reads 0.9970.997, i.e. the metric correctly reporting a signal-free condition. We therefore report the reference on the 5050 sentences of ≥5\geq 5 words recurring across distinct videos (116116 renditions; typically intro/outro scripts re-performed across a signer’s video series), which gives 0.8490.849, consistent with the Phoenix and ASL3DWord values. Both numbers are disclosed; all 1414 How2Sign checkpoints (0.890.89–1.001.00) lie above the 0.8490.849 reference.

F Coverage analyses and controls

Conditioning-space dispersion.

Two measures per corpus, computed on the same frozen text encoder the generators condition on (English CLIP-ViT-B/32 unless noted, so the numbers describe the geometry of the signal the denoiser receives; the last row re-measures CSL-Daily on the Chinese-CLIP text tower that the reported CSL-Daily models condition on): (a) within-train dispersion, the pairwise cosine among training-sentence embeddings (subsample of 4,0004{,}000 sentences, ∼\sim88M pairs); (b) coverage, each test sentence’s cosine to its nearest training neighbor (full pool). Both are reported raw (as the model sees them) and mean-centered (train centroid subtracted and renormalized, which removes the encoder’s anisotropy). XLM-R [3] mean-pooled embeddings are degenerate in the raw space (∼\sim0.990.99 cosine for every pair, the well-known cone effect) and are therefore reported centered only, as a direction-preserving control. Table S3 gives the full numbers behind Table 5.

Nearest-neighbor retrieval sweep.

For each test sentence we retrieve the nearest training sentence by cosine in the text-encoder space, take that training sample’s GT motion as the “prediction”, encode it with the dataset’s MoAE, and compute ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} and ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}} exactly as for a generator. The pool is a random subset of the training split of the stated size (full test split throughout). Table S4 lists the curves. On How2Sign the curve is flat at 0.970.97–1.001.00 over a 50×50\times pool increase; a per-sample check at the full pool shows the distribution of d⁡(retrieved,target)d(\text{retrieved},\text{target}) relative to random pairing is indistinguishable from the random-pairing null at every quantile, so no subpopulation of test sentences finds a matching training motion. On Phoenix-2014T the curve improves with pool size to the 0.8740.874 reference. On CSL-Daily, English CLIP gives a flat curve near 0.930.93, while Chinese-CLIP retrieves better neighbors at every pool size (0.888→0.8680.888\to 0.868, minimum 0.8540.854 at 99K) — the model-free signature of the encoder contamination discussed in the main text.

Text-shuffling control.

For each test sentence tit_{i} we generate with the sentence-conditioned MDM (guidance 3.03.0; How2Sign: the unfiltered 3131K checkpoint, row 6 of Tab. S1; Phoenix-2014T: row 6 of Table 3) under four conditions: (a) tit_{i} with seed s1s_{1}; (b) tit_{i} with seed s2s_{2}; (c) a random word permutation of tit_{i} with seed s1s_{1}; (d) a different test sentence tjt_{j} with seed s1s_{1} (matched seed). In the MoAE latent, dintrad_{\rm intra} is the mean distance (a)–(b), dshufd_{\rm shuf} the mean distance (a)–(c), and dinterd_{\rm inter} the mean distance (a)–(d). Sentences with fewer than three words cannot be meaningfully shuffled and are dropped (3131 of a 1,0001{,}000-sentence compute subsample on How2Sign; 11 of 642642 on Phoenix-2014T). ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} is computed for the original and the shuffled conditioning against the same GT. Table S5 gives the numbers behind Sec. 6.4: on How2Sign, replacing the sentence moves the output no more than re-sampling the noise (dinter/dintra=1.05d_{\rm inter}/d_{\rm intra}=1.05), whereas on Phoenix-2014T it moves it well beyond noise (1.351.35) and shuffling the words moves it less than a new seed (0.490.49).

Encoder-swap control.

The 2626K How2Sign clean regression model was retrained with a frozen T5-base encoder [18] in place of CLIP (all else equal; batch size 512512, T5 forward pass in fp32). Full test split (n=2,314n=2{,}314 sentences with valid SMPL-X fits, the set every How2Sign diagnostic uses): ρfaith=0.942\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.942, ρdiv=0.32\rho_{\mathrm{div}}=0.32, versus 0.9540.954 / 0.340.34 with CLIP; best evaluation loss 0.09200.0920 vs 0.09250.0925. The stronger encoder reaches the same solution and the same collapse.

Chinese-CLIP for CSL-Daily.

English CLIP on Chinese byte-pair tokens yields a within-train cosine of 0.880.88 (Tab. S3), i.e. nearly constant conditioning. All CSL-Daily generators and the retrieval sweep were therefore re-run with the Chinese-CLIP text tower [25] (CLS token after the contrastive projection; the projected space separates distinct sentences at cosine ≈0.79\approx 0.79, whereas mean-pooled hidden states form a new cone at 0.920.92 and are not used). Every CSL-Daily model improved by 0.050.05–0.120.12 in ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} under the swap (sentence 0.867→0.7980.867\to 0.798, keywords 0.870→0.7870.870\to 0.787, native gloss 0.836→0.7880.836\to 0.788, fused 0.865→0.7500.865\to 0.750, regression 0.872→0.7750.872\to 0.775); only the Chinese-CLIP numbers are reported in the main text. The dispersion measurement itself, re-run on the Chinese-CLIP tower (last row of Tab. S3), tells the same story: within-train cosine falls from 0.880.88 to 0.720.72 and centered coverage rises to 0.7100.710, between How2Sign and Phoenix-2014T — consistent with CSL-Daily’s intermediate model outcome.

G Frame-level DTW alignability

Protocol.

GT and generated sequences are forward-kinematics lifted to the same 4444 upper-body 33D joints the MoAE consumes (root zeroed, T=100T=100), but compared per frame: the frame distance is the L2 distance between the two 44×344\times 3 joint sets, and the alignment cost is the mean frame distance along the optimal dynamic-time-warping path. We report the ratio of this cost for the generation and its own GT to the cost for the generation and the GT of an unrelated sentence (DTW/random; 11 = chance). The equal-timestamp variant uses the diagonal path instead of the DTW path (diag/random). The human–human baseline applies the identical statistic to two GT renditions of the same sentence (4040 same-text groups per corpus, pooled train++test); the generation statistic uses 4040 test sentences (seed 4242; unseen sentences for CSL-Daily), a sample disjoint from the four rendered sentences per corpus.

Findings.

Table S6 gives the statistics behind Sec. 6.2. (i) Two humans are far from frame-identical (0.740.74 on Phoenix-2014T, 0.590.59 on CSL-Daily), so a single GT video demands more consistency than signers exhibit. (ii) Generation sits one band above the human distribution on both corpora; normalized to each corpus’s own human mean, Phoenix-2014T stands at 1.16×1.16\times and CSL-Daily at 1.29×1.29\times, the same ordering as the sequence-level MoAE verdicts. (iii) The best-aligned tail of the generation distribution (p10) reaches the human mean, and it is populated by the densest conditions: in the 4040-sentence Phoenix sample, the broadcast sign-off “ich wünsche noch einen schönen abend” occupies two of the three best-aligned slots (0.680.68, 0.700.70), and among the four rendered Phoenix sentences the recurring opener is the only one inside the human band (0.660.66; the three non-formulaic ones sit at 0.930.93–0.990.99). (iv) Without DTW, timing offsets masquerade as pose error: the equal-timestamp ratio is 0.980.98 / 0.970.97 for generations and inflates even the human–human pairs to 0.920.92 / 0.780.78. GT-timeline frame strips therefore overstate mismatch, and all figures show DTW-matched pairs.

Rendered examples.

Figure S3 shows the two rendered sentences not included in Fig. 3, at the generation median (CSL-Daily) and in the typical non-formulaic Phoenix range. Of the four rendered sentences per corpus, those shown are: Phoenix-2014T — “und nun die wettervorhersage für morgen donnerstag den dritten dezember” (0.6630.663; main Fig. 3a) and “teilweise kräftiger regen zieht heute nacht über uns ostwärts” (0.9750.975; Fig. S3a); CSL-Daily —

性格，既不坚固也不是一成不变，而是活动变化着的。 (“Character is neither fixed nor immutable, but active and changing.”; 0.6990.699; main Fig. 3b) and

合肥气温低，你骑自行车上学一定很冷。 (“Hefei is cold; cycling to school must be freezing.”; 0.7430.743; Fig. S3b). None of these sentences appears in any extraction prompt.

H Code-level audit of Progressive Transformers

A prominent Phoenix SLP system, Progressive Transformers [19], reports better BLEU than our checkpoints. Reading the released code, we find three inference/evaluation paths that leak ground-truth timing or length into the reported protocol; the two most important are (L1) the predicted counter scalar is overwritten by the GT counter at every decoder step, and (L2) the inference output length is set to the GT sequence length rather than learned via a stop signal.

PT on the clean Phoenix-2014T SMPL-X data (Sec. 6.5).

We retrained the official PT code on the same SOKE SMPL-X Phoenix data as our MDM and regression models (FK-lifted to the 4444-joint 33D space the MoAE consumes) and ran inference twice on the same checkpoint. Under fair inference (counter and length governed by the model’s own predictions) PT collapses: ρfaith=0.9999\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.9999, ρdiv=0.025\rho_{\mathrm{div}}=0.025, dinter=0.08d_{\rm inter}=0.08 against a GT spread of 3.263.26. Under the paper’s leaky protocol (GT counter and length supplied at inference) ρfaith=0.9974\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.9974 and ρdiv=0.223\rho_{\mathrm{div}}=0.223: the leak inflates apparent output diversity ∼\sim9×9\times while leaving faithfulness at chance. MDM (0.8390.839) and the clean regression model (0.8110.811) are faithful on the identical data. The remainder of this section reports the earlier leaky-vs-fair experiment on PT’s own pose representation, which reaches the same conclusion.

Leaky-vs-fair experiment.

We retrained PT’s released code on Phoenix-2014T at the paper’s native data scale and “best T2P” configuration, with no changes to architecture, loss, training, or inference logic, then ran inference twice on the same checkpoint over all 632632 test sentences: once with leaks (L1)+(L2) intact (“leaky”), once with all three leaks off (“fair”, counter and length governed purely by the model’s predictions). Outputs were encoded with the Phoenix MediaPipe MoAE (Sec. D) and dinterd_{\rm inter}/ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}}/ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} computed on the full test split (Tab. S7).

Representation and extraction.

The independent PT retrainings cited in the main text use OpenPose-derived 3D joints [10, 24] or a SMPL-X representation [26], and PT’s original pipeline uses OpenPose. For this experiment we extract Phoenix poses with MediaPipe Holistic, because OpenPose’s released codebase has very limited maintenance and is difficult to deploy in a modern environment. This extraction is imperfect: across the Phoenix train split, 28.6%28.6\% of left-hand and 23.9%23.9\% of right-hand frames are returned with no detection and are interpolated (see hand-detection notes below). We therefore use the leaky-vs-fair result only as a within-checkpoint comparison (the checkpoint, and any extraction artefact, is held fixed across the two inference passes, so the contrast still isolates the leak), and do not report absolute PT performance from this retraining; the SMPL-X retraining above uses the same clean data as every other Phoenix model in the paper.

Findings.

(i) The leak measurably changes PT’s output. Toggling the GT-timing/length leak on the same trained checkpoint inflates the inter-sample spread dinterd_{\rm inter} from 0.0310.031 to 0.2070.207 and the diversity ratio ρdiv\rho_{\mathrm{div}} from 0.0130.013 to 0.0890.089, a roughly sevenfold change (Tab. S7), while ρfaith\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays at chance (0.999→0.9960.999\to 0.996). Because the checkpoint is held fixed across the two inference passes, this isolates the leak: the GT-aligned timing it supplies materially affects the generated motion and any statistic computed from it, without making the motion any more faithful to its sentence. (ii) Fair inference does not learn end-of-sequence in our text-to-pose setting. Without the GT counter, the predicted counter never crosses the stop threshold: every one of the 632632 test samples runs to the 300300-frame cap, while GT lengths range from 33 to 8989 frames. Under text conditioning, PT’s continuous-output decoder relies on (L1) for inference-time length supervision; a gloss-conditioned PT, whose input already encodes sign count, retains a partial length signal (leak-free gloss-to-pose PT reaches BLEU-4 4.044.04; 10).

The rest of this section gives the full L1–L3 enumeration, the training setup for the leaky-vs-fair experiment, and the supporting pose-extractor, hand-detection, and bug-fix notes needed to make the released code execute under modern tooling.

Three inference- and evaluation-time leaks.

Inspection of the released repository identifies the following three paths through which GT timing or length information enters PT’s reported numerical protocol:

  1. (L1)

    search.py:55–63: at every decoder step the predicted counter scalar c^t\hat{c}_{t} is overwritten with the GT counter ct∗c^{*}_{t} before being fed back. The author comment in the file reads: “Drive the timing by giving the GT timing”.

  2. (L2)

    search.py:46: the inference output length is assigned from the GT target length rather than learned via a stop signal.

  3. (L3)

    Configs/Base.yaml:25,29: the only validation/early-stopping metric is the DTW score itself, so the reported quantitative results come from this GT-aligned distance.

Training setup and toggle list.

Training matched the paper’s data scale (∼\sim7 0007\,000 training sequences) and the published “best T2P” configuration (22 encoder/decoder layers, 44 heads, 512512 embedding dim, MSE loss, future-prediction FP=10\mathrm{FP}{=}10, Gaussian-noise augmentation rate 55). Training reached lrmin\mathrm{lr}_{\min} at step 14501450, with best validation DTW =15.76=15.76 at step 450450. The “leaky” inference configuration in Tab. S7 leaves (L1)+(L2) intact (matching the paper’s reported protocol up to BLEU back-translation); the “fair” configuration disables all three leaks listed above (counter is purely autoregressive, output length is governed by a predicted-counter stop rule capped at the global 300300-frame limit, and the DTW-aligned distance is no longer used as the model-selection metric). Both inference passes were run over all 632632 test sentences on the same trained checkpoint.

Pose extraction divergence from the original paper.

Saunders et al. [19] use OpenPose followed by 2D-to-3D inverse-kinematics lifting; we substitute MediaPipe Holistic upper-body keypoints because the OpenPose pipeline is impractical to re-deploy on contemporary GPU toolchains and the extraction is not released. The two extractors differ in keypoint set and 2D-vs-3D representation, but the total paired-sample budget is identical at ∼\sim7 0007\,000 training sequences, so the leak audit still applies; what we cannot precisely reproduce are the absolute pose-space FID values (which depend on extraction).

Hand-detection failure rate.

MediaPipe Holistic produces all-zero hand keypoints when detection confidence is below threshold. Across the Phoenix train split, the mean per-video fraction of fully-missing left-hand frames is 28.6%28.6\% (max 100%100\%); for the right hand 23.9%23.9\% (max 84%84\%). We linearly-interpolate within each clip and fall back to the corresponding body wrist when an entire hand is missing throughout, so PT does not train against zero-hand targets.

Bug fixes required to run the released code under a modern deep-learning toolchain.

We applied six small patches to make the released code execute under the current toolchain. None of the patches touch the architecture, loss, training loop, validation loss/DTW computation, model selection, or inference/search code: the model and training-relevant files (model.py, transformer_layers.py, encoders.py, decoders.py, embeddings.py, loss.py, search.py, data.py, batch.py, vocabulary.py) are byte-for-byte the released versions. The patches are: removing the deprecated verbose kwarg from ReduceLROnPlateau (builders.py:137); fixing an undefined train_output reference (prediction.py:73); removing a redundant FP-cut on the inference output already cut in search.py:greedy (prediction.py:74); making plot_videos.py:47 adaptive to MediaPipe’s 6767-joint layout; wrapping produce_validation_video in try/except to swallow bone-graph mismatches at validation-video render time (the _save_checkpoint call lies outside the try block, so model selection is unaffected); and adding weights_only=False to torch.load (helpers.py:202). Total diff vs the upstream repo: 3232 lines added, 2020 lines removed across 55 files.

Reproducibility.

The patched code, training and audit scripts, configurations, and all per-sample inference outputs are available alongside the paper. Reproducing Tab. S7 end-to-end requires only a single GPU.
